info.bio:
Patricia Lee "Patti" Smith (nacida el 30 de diciembre de 1946) es una cantante y poetisa estadounidense.

Saltó a la fama durante el movimiento punk con su álbum debut de 1975 Horses. Llamada "La madrina del punk", trajo un punto de vista feminista e intelectual a la música punk y se convirtió en una de las artistas más influyentes dentro de la música rock, integrándola con un estilo de poesía beat.

Sus alusiones introdujeron la poesía francesa del siglo XIX a la juventud norteamericana

scenes.name: Punk neoyorquino del CBGB
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, Blondie, The Heartbreakers: una escena que, como advirtió James Wolcott en 1975 («Un impulso conservador en el nuevo underground del rock»), se presentaba como el retorno de algo perdido. Los Ramones agotan su idea en dos discos, los Heartbreakers son Dr. Feelgood con heroína y hasta Television bebe del acid rock de la costa oeste. La revista Punk de Legs McNeil proclama «¡Muerte a esa mierda disco!» y rechaza al hipster como «negro blanco».
scenes.family: Antecedentes: punk, art rock, kraut y glam

scenes.name: New wave neoyorquina
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: 1976 es un año bisagra: los sellos independientes revitalizan la industria y nuevos géneros la escena, una revolución comparable a la de 1966. Los jóvenes de los setenta, sin sueños tras la derrota de la contracultura, canalizan su aburrimiento en un sonido crudo emparentado con el garage. Nueva York es la capital: el CBGB's y el Max's Kansas City. Patti Smith, Richard Hell (el profeta: «Blank Generation» y la ética punk), Television (Marquee Moon, que define la estética de la new wave), Tom Verlaine, y los Ramones, que tocan rock'n'roll inepto a velocidad supersónica e inventan el género más importante del último cuarto de siglo.

podcast.title: Avant-garde Poetry Readings (Since 1971)
podcast.body: Since 1971, Patti Smith, a "thin, intense poet from New Jersey," had been performing hip avant-garde poetry readings on St. Mark's Place in The Village, laying the groundwork for her musical career. "She had been giving these hip avant-garde poetry readings on St. Mark's Place in the Village since 1971."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paris Cemetery Epiphany (1972)
podcast.body: In the summer of 1972, Patti Smith, then an aspiring poet from New York, visited the Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris. While at the graveside of The Doors singer Jim Morrison, she experienced an epiphany that led her to believe she could be more than just a poet. Jim Morrison "apparently appeared to her" during this transformative moment.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Claim for First True Punk Rock Record (1974)
podcast.body: Many music historians credit Patti Smith's 1974 debut single, particularly its original B-side (believed to be "Piss Factory"), as the "first true punk rock record." This significant independent recording directly stemmed from her profound graveside vision in Paris two years prior.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Debut Single Release (June 5, 1974)
podcast.body: On June 5, 1974, Patti Smith independently released a thousand copies of a seven-inch single on Robert Mapplethorpe's small label. The B-side, "Piss Factory," gained significant attention from the New York avant-garde. "So on June 5th, 1974, Patty released a thousand copies of a seven-inch single on Mapplethorpe's tiny independent label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influential Albums (1975-1979)
podcast.body: Between 1975 and 1979, Patti Smith released four very important and extremely influential albums. These works were bold, filled with strong statements and opinions on diverse topics such as religion, racism, feminist principles, and the state of society, profoundly changing the lives of many female punks and future Riot Girls, as well as many guys. "She released four very important and extremely influential albums between 1975 and 1979."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Prominent Artist in New York Scene (1975)
podcast.body: Patti Smith was identified as one of the leading artists in the emerging New York music scene in 1975, a movement centered around the legendary CBGB club. "En Nueva York estaban emergiendo una escena liderada por bandas como Ramones, Televisión, Patie Smith, Suicide, Blondie or Tolkien Hets."

podcast.title: Early Punk Priestess Gig (1976)
podcast.body: Patti Smith, described as a "punk priestess," played an influential show in New York City a couple of months before the Ramones' pivotal appearance in England. Her performance was an early, significant manifestation of the burgeoning punk rock phenomenon in the US. "Outside of a show, punk priestess Patty Smith had played a couple of months earlier, the Ramones appearance would be England's first proper exposure to US style punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Debut (1976)
podcast.body: Patti Smith made her UK debut in May 1976. "Patty Smith made her UK debut in May."

podcast.title: Marriage and Retirement (1980)
podcast.body: Patti Smith married Fred Sonic Smith, a member of MC5 and her collaborator in the 1980s, in 1980, shortly after the release of her album *Wave*. Following their marriage, she largely retired from public life to live with Fred and raise their children in Detroit. "They got married in 1980 Not long after Wave was released and then she kind of just retired From public life to go live with Fred and to raise their children in Detroit."

podcast.title: Times Square Soundtrack Contribution (1980)
podcast.body: Patti Smith was included on the soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square*. This soundtrack was notable for being one of the pioneering compilations to feature the emerging alternative music of the day, including punk rock and new wave. "There was Lou Reed and the Cure and Patty Smith and Susie Quattro."

podcast.title: Fred "Sonic" Smith's Death (1994)
podcast.body: Patty and Fred "Sonic" Smith remained married for six years after co-producing *Dream of Life*, until Fred died of a heart attack in 1994. This marked the end of their personal and creative partnership. "Patty and Fred remained married for six more years until Fred died of a heart attack in 1994."

podcast.title: Last Performance at CBGB (October 15, 2006)
podcast.body: Patti Smith fittingly performed on the last night of CBGB, October 15, 2006. During her performance, she read a list of deceased musicians who had graced the club's stage, including Joey Ramone, and sang "Elegie" as a poignant farewell to the iconic venue. "She got up on the stage and she read off a list of musicians who had played there, who were no longer living Joey Ramone being one of them."

podcast.title: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction (2007)
podcast.body: Patti Smith was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2007 by Zach De La Rocha of Rage Against the Machine. De La Rocha lauded her for revitalizing rock music, noting that it "was getting too slick for its own good when Paddy Smith burst on the scene and tore it apart." "She shrieked and howled literate yet street savvy lyrics, unflinchingly confronting topics from religion to the beat movement."

podcast.title: 2019 Benefit Performance with Stuart Copeland
podcast.body: In 2019, Patty Smith performed at New York's Public Theater with Stuart Copeland of The Police and the collective Choir, Choir, Choir. This concert was a benefit to raise awareness for immigrants struggling at the Mexican border, where they performed her anthem "People Have the Power." The event was characterized as a "do-it-yourself happening," aligning with Smith's brand. "The occasion was a benefit to raise awareness of immigrants struggling at the Mexican border."

podcast.title: "Godmother of Punk" Still Performing
podcast.body: Patty Smith, often referred to as the "Godmother of Punk," continues to perform well into her career, almost half a century after her debut at CBGB. This demonstrates her enduring legacy and active presence in music. "As for Patty Smith, the so-called Godmother of Punk is still performing to this day, almost a half century after she made her CBGB debut."

podcast.title: "Godmother of Punk" Title
podcast.body: Within a few years of initiating her musical endeavors, Patti Smith earned the esteemed title "the godmother of punk," highlighting her influential role in the nascent punk rock scene.

podcast.title: Accidental Recording of Piss Factory
podcast.body: The recording of "Piss Factory" was somewhat accidental. Patti Smith and Lenny Kay had booked studio time to record a cover of the Jimi Hendrix song "Hey Joe," but they finished early. With the remaining time, they recorded "Piss Factory," a track that recounted Smith's experiences working in a doll factory. "Piss Factory was sort of an accident. They had booked time to record a cover of the Jimmy Hendrix song Hey Joe and finished early."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Admiration for Mark Linkous
podcast.body: Patti Smith was noted as an admirer of Mark Linkous, the songwriter and frontman for Sparklehorse, highlighting his respected status among his peers in the music industry. "He had fans of the flaming lips, and metric of the Silver Sun pickups, and Patty Smith and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Great Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of the 90s: Part 2

podcast.title: Called a "Punk" (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, as the term "punk rock" was being used liberally and carelessly, Patti Smith was among the artists, including Aerosmith, Bruce Springsteen, and The Rolling Stones, who were called a "punk." "By the middle of the 70s, the term was being thrown around very carelessly, very liberally. Patty Smith was called a punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Career Breakthrough
podcast.body: The unexpected success of her debut single "Piss Factory" propelled Patti Smith towards a major label record deal. This marked her transition into a genuine recording artist and established her as a leading icon in the burgeoning New York punk rock scene, and subsequently, the broader rock scene. "This little bit of success set Patty on the road to becoming a genuine recording artist, nailing a major label record deal and becoming a leading icon on the New York punk rock scene, and then, well, the rock scene in general."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Celebrity Photographer
podcast.body: Robert Mapplethorpe photographed Patti Smith in the 1970s, contributing to album covers. "I think of Robert Mapplethorb's photos of Patty Smith back in the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chelsea Hotel Guest
podcast.body: Patti Smith was listed as one of the musicians who were frequent guests or residents at the Chelsea Hotel. "Bob Dylan, Patty Smith, Leonard Cohen, Janice Joplin, Jimmy Henrichs, Tom Waits, Jim Morrison, Jeff Beck, Johnny Mitchell, Alice Cooper, the guys in Pink Floyd, and many, many others."

podcast.title: Cited as a Rock Poet
podcast.body: Patti Smith is listed as one of the rare "poets in rock," alongside other prominent lyricists. "There's Dylan, Springsteen, Patty Smith, Jim Morrison, Bono, certainly, maybe Lou Reed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Lenny Kaye
podcast.body: Patti Smith met record store clerk Lenny Kaye, who would play guitar improvisations while she recited her poems, leading to their musical collaboration. "Then she met Lenny Kay, a record store clerk, and he would noodle on his guitar as Patty recited her poems."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Malcolm Burn
podcast.body: Malcolm Burn has produced and engineered for Patti Smith. "With Dan's help Malcolm has had gigs producing an engineering for Iggy Pop and Patty Smith and Bob Dylan and Blue Road View and Midnight Oil and junk house and John Mellon Camp in many many more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovery by Jerry Brande
podcast.body: Patti Smith was one of the significant artists discovered by Jerry Brande, a renowned talent scout during the 1970s who also discovered Joe Brieaz. "había descubierto a gente muy importante como como patia esmíci."

podcast.title: Early Artistic Collaboration
podcast.body: Patti Smith, originally a poet and music writer, often performed readings with her friend Lenny Kaye, who would "noodle around on a guitar in the background." This informal collaboration eventually led to their first recording. "Patty was a poet and music writer, who often did readings with her friends, record-storkler Lenny Kay, noodling around on a guitar in the background."

podcast.title: Early Career - "Free Verse" Punk at CBGB
podcast.body: Patty Smith was identified as one of the CBGB artists in the 1970s known for her "free verse" style, distinguishing her within the nascent punk scene. This lyrical approach defined her early contributions to the genre. "to the free verse of Patty Smith"

podcast.title: Early Career and Appearance
podcast.body: Described as a "skinny poet from New Jersey who looked like a female version of Keith Richards," Smith performed club gigs in some of the "scusiest venues in town." "We have to get back to this skinny poet from New Jersey who looked like a female version of Keith Richards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career as Poet and Writer
podcast.body: Patti Smith began her career as a poet and music writer, often performing readings. She was frequently accompanied by her friend, record store clerk Lenny Kay, who would improvise on guitar in the background. "Patty was a poet and music writer who often did readings with her friend, record store clerk Lenny Kay, noodling around on a guitar in the background."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Performances at CBGB
podcast.body: Patti Smith was one of the key artists performing regularly at CBGB by the summer of 1974, contributing significantly to the club's burgeoning reputation as a center for the emerging punk movement. "By the summer of 1974, Hilly's bar, now known just as CBGB to everyone, was hosting not just television, but the Ramones, Patty Smith, Suicide, Blondie, Talking Heads, the Heartbreakers, and a bunch of other groups."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 5: (60-51)

podcast.title: Early UK Punk Performance
podcast.body: Patty Smith, referred to as a "punk priestess," played a show in England a couple of months before The Ramones' July 1976 appearances. Her performance was one of the few instances of US-style punk rock exposure in the UK before the Ramones' more significant impact. "Outside of a show, punk priestess Patty Smith had played a couple of months earlier, the Ramones appearance would be England's first proper exposure to US style punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Embraced by New York Avant-garde
podcast.body: Patti Smith was recognized as an "artsy soulmate" for other experimental New York artists like Television, and her music was embraced when bands like Pere Ubu brought their Cleveland sound to New York. "When Ubu brought this music to New York, home of artsy soulmates like television and Patsy Smith, they were embraced."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Godmother of Riot Grrrl
podcast.body: Patti Smith is widely considered the godmother of all the Riot Grrrls. She was a punk poet, author, and musician who first surfaced in New York City even before the punk movement fully took hold, releasing four significant and influential albums between 1975 and 1979. "But if there's a godmother to all the Riot Girls, it's gotta be Patty Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gratitude to Clive Davis
podcast.body: At her Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction, Patti Smith sincerely thanked Clive Davis of Arista Records for giving her a chance, later posting a photo of them together on Instagram to express her continued appreciation. "On that night she thanked Clive Davis of Aresda for giving her a chance. I think she really meant it too."

podcast.title: Hesitation to Collaborate
podcast.body: Initially, Patti Smith was hesitant to write "Because the Night" because she preferred to write songs that were "completely hers," showcasing her strong artistic integrity and dedication to her own creative control. "She was just hesitant to write a song that was not completely hers."

For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Hilly Crystal's Impression
podcast.body: Hilly Crystal, the owner of CBGB, was deeply impressed by Patti Smith's charisma and performance, describing her as possessing "magnetism." He found her capable of staying on pitch, bending notes expertly, and communicating effectively, making her one of the few artists he could listen to repeatedly. "She may not have been a singer but she sure sounded like one. She stayed on pitch, she bent the notes just right, she sang real well, she communicated."

podcast.title: Icon of New York Punk and Rock Scene
podcast.body: The early success of "Piss Factory" enabled Patti Smith to secure a major label record deal and swiftly establish herself as a leading icon within the New York punk rock scene, and subsequently, the broader rock scene. She inspired many with her defiant perspective on life and her unprecedented vocal style. "This little bit of success set Patty on the road to becoming a genuine recording artist, nailing a major label record deal and becoming a leading icon on the New York punk rock scene and then, well, the rock scene in general."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Independent Release Success
podcast.body: Following its accidental recording, "Piss Factory" was pressed as a one-off seven-inch single, with a limited run of a thousand copies. These copies were strategically placed in independent bookstores and record sellers, where they sold out almost instantly. This initial success was pivotal, setting Smith on the path to becoming a genuine recording artist. "They pressed up a thousand copies and seated it at independent bookstores and record sellers. It sold out almost instantly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence and Unique Style
podcast.body: Patti Smith was an inspiration to both men and women due to her defiant "I don't give a crap" attitude and her pioneering vocal style. Her approach to music was entirely unique, distinguishing her from any vocalist heard before her time. "Patty was an inspiration to so many women and men with her techno prisoners I don't give a crap view of the world, the universe, and beyond."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Legs McNeill's "Punk" Fanzine
podcast.body: Patti Smith was an artist from the underground music scene on the "scuzzy side of Manhattan" who inspired Legs McNeill. Her work, along with that of others, was part of the musical landscape that McNeill loved and documented in his seminal "Punk" fanzine. "Not only was he into the garage band music of the 1960s, he loved the velvet underground and Lou Reed and Patty Smith and the New York Dolls and Iggy Pop."

podcast.title: Influence on Michael Stipe
podcast.body: Michael Stipe, at 15, was profoundly influenced by Patti Smith after reading about her in *Cream* magazine and purchasing *Horses* on its release day. Stipe noted that punk rockers like Smith conveyed the idea that "you did not have to be special to start a band," a concept that particularly resonated with him. "He said that the punk rockers like Patty gave him the idea that they were not special And that you did not have to be special to start a band."

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Because the Night"
podcast.body: Patti Smith penned the lyrics for "Because the Night" in a single night while waiting for a phone call from her future husband, Fred 'Sonic' Smith. This personal experience of anticipation and desire infused the song with its powerful emotional and sexual themes. "Patty, again, known to agonize at length over her lyrics, wrote because the night in one night as she waited by the phone for her future husband, Fred Sonic Smith to call."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Inspirational and Unconventional Artist
podcast.body: Patti Smith inspired both men and women with her distinctive "I don't give a crap view of the world, the universe, and beyond," and her uncompromising approach to her art. Her vocal delivery was described as unlike anything heard before, embodying a spirit of doing things her own way. "Patty was an inspiration to so many women and men with her techno prisoners I don't give a crap view of the world, the universe, and beyond."

podcast.title: Last Words at CBGB Closing
podcast.body: Patti Smith, an artist deeply associated with CBGB, appropriately delivered the final words on the club's closing night, October 15, 2006, marking the end of an era for the legendary punk venue. "And Patty Smith, appropriately, had the last words."

podcast.title: Marriage to Fred "Sonic" Smith
podcast.body: Just before the release of her 1979 album *Wave*, Patty Smith met Fred "Sonic" Smith, who was the former guitar player for the Detroit proto-punk band, the MC5. They fell in love and got married, and Fred later co-produced her 1988 comeback album, *Dream of Life*, which was their only musical collaboration. "Just before the release of WAVE Patty Smith met Fred Sonic Smith, former guitar player for the Detroit Proto-Punk band, the MC5."

podcast.title: Poet and Rock Challenger
podcast.body: Patti Smith, a poet, uniquely utilized rock music as a vehicle to recite, scream, and challenge the traditional roles assigned to women in music. Her approach infused rock with a poetic and rebellious spirit, expanding its expressive potential. "Patismite, una poeta causaba el rock como un vehículo para recitar, gritar y desafiar el rol tradicional de la mujer en la música."

podcast.title: Poetic Approach to Songwriting
podcast.body: Patti Smith is characterized as a "poet who sings her poetry," known for her belief in music as a means for reflection and societal change. She meticulously "labored over her lyrics," emphasizing that "the words within them matter" to achieve her artistic vision. "She wrote songs from the perspective of someone who believes in music as a means of reflection and the force of change."

For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Poetic Foundations
podcast.body: Patti Smith identified herself as a poet first, sharing insights from her 1976 European tour about her inspirations. She confessed to struggling with grammar and extensively studied authors like Henry Miller, Mickey Spillane, Burroughs, and Rimbaud to learn sentence construction, while also studying T.S. Eliot for rhythm and music, alongside listening to Jajuca tapes, Berber tapes, and "the great primitives, American Rock and Roll." "Art was a great revelation to me and then all my life it's like still that freedom I had as a child."

"Suzy Su, of Suzy in the Banshee's, members of the Slitz, Pauli Styrene of X-Ray Specks, Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders, Patty Smith, and so many more. They were all pioneers and they all inspired many people, women, but also men, to do what they did."

podcast.body: Patti Smith was one of the artists from the burgeoning New York scene who secured a record deal, enabling her music to be distributed and heard beyond New York City. podcast.title: Semi-Retirement in the 1980s
podcast.body: After finishing the 1970s with her *Wave* album, Patty Smith spent most of the 1980s in semi-retirement from music. She married Fred "Sonic" Smith, former guitarist for the proto-punk band MC5, and raised their two children in Michigan, just north of Detroit. "And Patty spent most of the 80s semi-retired from music, raising their two kids in Michigan just north of Detroit."

podcast.title: Suggestion to Record (Robert Mapplethorpe)
podcast.body: Artist Robert Mapplethorpe, a friend of Patti Smith, suggested that she record her poetry readings to sell in "cooler bookshops" in The Village, which led to the recording of her first single. "This led to a suggestion by her friend, an artist named Robert Mapplethorpe, that she makes some recordings of these poetry readings that she could maybe sell in some of the cooler bookshops in the village."

podcast.title: Transition to Musical Career
podcast.body: Following her pivotal experience in Paris, Patti Smith returned to the United States and began incorporating a guitar player and a piano player into her poetry readings. This shift marked the beginning of her musical journey, leading to an increasing number of gigs and attracting the attention of record companies within a few years.

xref.title: Graveside Inspiration for Patti Smith (1972)
xref.body: In the summer of 1972, Patti Smith visited Jim Morrison's graveside at the Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris. During this visit, she experienced an epiphany that inspired her to pursue a musical career beyond poetry, with Morrison "apparently appearing to her" in that moment.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Meeting and Formation (Sacramento 1972-1975)
xref.body: Erick perkaiser (Lux interior) and Kristi Marlena Wallace (Poison Ivy) met in Sacramento in 1972. They were drawn together by a shared passion for horror movies and record collecting. By 1975, they had formed The Cramps and began performing at venues like CBGB, sharing stages with bands such as The Ramones, Blondie, Talking Heads, and Patti Smith. "They met in Sacramento back in 1972, and were drawn together by their love of horror movies and record collecting. By 1975, they'd formed the Cramps and were playing places like CBGB alongside their hormones and blondie and talking heads and patty smith and so many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Gig (November 1975)
xref.body: The Sex Pistols played their first gig in November 1975, the same month Patti Smith released her influential debut album "Horses." They were contemporaries of The Slits and a foundational band of the punk movement. "That was the same month the sex pistols played their first gig"

xref.title: First Album Release (Mid-1976)
xref.body: The Ramones released their first album approximately six months after Patti Smith's debut "Horses" in November 1975. They were a key band in the early New York City punk scene. "and a good six months before the Ramones released their first album."

xref.title: Assault on Patti Smith's Brother – December 9, 1978
xref.body: On December 9, 1978, Sid got into a fight with the brother of singer Patti Smith during a night out and slashed his face with a beer bottle. He was arrested on felony assault charges and sent back to Rikers Island. "They get into a fight and Sid slashes the guy's face with a beer bottle."

xref.title: Death (November 1994)
xref.body: Fred 'Sonic' Smith, a member of MC5 and husband of "punk priestess" Patti Smith, died in November 1994 from a heart attack. "Fred Sonic Smith, member of the MC-5 and husband of punk priestess Patty Smith, heart attack, November 1994."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Meg White's Marriage (2009)
xref.body: Meg White married Jackson Smith, the son of punk legend Patti Smith, in 2009. The wedding ceremony took place in Jack White's backyard in Nashville. "And then when Meg married a guy named Jackson Smith, the son of punk legend, Patty Smith in 2009, the ceremony took place in Jack's backyard in Nashville."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tom Verlaine Death (January 28, 2023) – Prostate Cancer, Age 73; Helped CBGB Become Ground Zero for Punk
xref.body: Tom Verlaine co-founded Television and in 1973 helped Hilly Kristal — owner of a scuzzy bar on Bleecker Street in a then-terrible part of New York — to let Television play a Sunday night residency. This decision catalyzed CBGB into becoming ground zero for New York punk and, by chain reaction, the entire international punk movement. Television produced two critically acclaimed albums before breaking up in 1978. Verlaine subsequently collaborated with Patti Smith, worked with James Iha of the Smashing Pumpkins, had a song covered by David Bowie, and was involved in a 1992 Television reunion album. He was scheduled to produce Jeff Buckley's second album — a project ended when Buckley drowned in the Mississippi River in 1997. Verlaine was diagnosed with prostate cancer at some point in the 2000s; it metastasized. He died January 28, 2023, age 73. "That was the catalyst for making CBGB ground zero for the world of New York punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Assault on Todd Smith's Girlfriend
xref.body: On December 5, 1978, while supervised by Rockets Red Glare at a club, Sid Vicious got into a fight using a beer bottle with the girlfriend of Todd Smith, the brother of singer Patti Smith. He was arrested, charged with assault, and sent to Riker's Island. "On December 5th, he went to a club under the supervision of Rockets Red Glare and got into a beer bottle fight with the girlfriend of Todd Smith, the brother of singer Patty Smith."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Name Origin
xref.body: The name "The Smiths" was deliberately chosen because Morrissey and Marr couldn't think of anything more plain or boring, making a statement against the fancy names of other Alt Rock bands of the early 80s like Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark and Depeche Mode. It was also a homage to New York poet Patti Smith, one of Morrissey's heroes, and possibly a nod to a 1960s Manchester nightclub called Mr. Smiths. "They chose the name the Smiths because they couldn't think of anything more plain or anything more boring. That was very deliberate."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Diverse Production and Engineering Work
xref.body: With the assistance of Daniel Lanois, Malcolm Burn has produced and engineered for a variety of artists including Iggy Pop, Patti Smith, Bob Dylan, Blue Road View, Midnight Oil, Junkhouse, and John Mellencamp. "With Dan's help Malcolm has had gigs producing an engineering for Iggy Pop and Patty Smith and Bob Dylan and Blue Road View and Midnight Oil and junk house and John Mellon Camp in many many more."

xref.title: Embraced by New York Avant-garde
xref.body: Television was recognized as an "artsy soulmate" for other experimental New York artists like Patti Smith, and their music was embraced when bands like Pere Ubu brought their Cleveland sound to New York. "When Ubu brought this music to New York, home of artsy soulmates like television and Patsy Smith, they were embraced."

xref.body: The Velvet Underground is credited with awakening and influencing a wide array of prominent artists and bands, including David Bowie, Roxy Music, The Doors, Patti Smith, Iggy Pop and the Stooges, U2, Joy Division, The Pixies, The Sex Pistols, Talking Heads, The Cure, Kraftwerk, R.E.M., Simple Minds, The Strokes, and The Psychedelic Furs, whose name derived from a Velvet Underground song.
